title: Inside the network: gradient size by layer, input features as filters, and what the last layer does to the classes
summary: These Playground figures look inside a model instead of at its score: how large the gradient is in each parameter during training, how depth changes the gradient reaching the first layer, what each input feature looks like as a picture, and how the final-layer embedding separates two classes.

media.alt: A log-scale line chart of the gradient norm reaching the first hidden layer against epoch, 0 to 25. The blue curve for two hidden layers starts near twenty and falls to about 0.05, with sawtooth steps. The orange curve for eight hidden layers starts near 0.3, falls similarly, and jumps up to about twenty at the last epochs.

read_the_figure.question: Is the learning signal reaching the early layers, and is it stable?
read_the_figure.axes: Gradient figures: epoch (horizontal) against the L2 norm of a gradient on a log scale from 1e-3 to 1e2 (vertical). Feature figure: seven small panels, each the input plane coloured by one feature value (red positive, blue negative). Embedding figure: a 2D projection of the last hidden layer, one dot per sample, two classes in red and blue.
look_at: The sawtooth: within each epoch the gradient steps up and down because the points are different mini-batches or recorded before and after a step. Read the envelope, not single points.

Depth comparison: at the start the eight-layer curve is about two orders of magnitude below the two-layer curve; this is vanishing gradient in one picture. Late in training the eight-layer curve jumps by about two decades, a sign of instability.

Per-parameter figure: six lines for weights and biases of three layers of the ODE function network. The weight gradients of the last layer are largest, biases smallest; all fall by three to four decades then rise sharply over the last epochs.
Feature filters: x and y are ramps, x2 and y2 are bowls, xy is a saddle, sin x and sin y are bands. Any model on these inputs is a combination of these seven pictures.

Embedding: the discrete network separates the classes into two tight points (separability printed as 1.0), the continuous Neural ODE keeps a curved spread with overlap (separability 0.901). The exact definition of the score is not printed on the figure.
read_the_figure.proves: A flat or tiny gradient in early layers means they are barely learning; a sudden rise means a loss spike is coming. Features define what the model can express. An embedding with well separated classes shows the last layer has done its job, but a continuous model may separate less cleanly and still be a better dynamical model.
if_wrong: Gradients below 1e-6: those parameters will not move; look at initialization, activation saturation or depth.
A late jump of several decades: the gradient is unstable; clip it or lower the learning rate.
A label such as 'pre-clip' on the axis: the plotted gradient is before clipping, so the step actually taken is smaller than it looks.
An embedding separated into two points: all information except class has been discarded, which is fine for classification and wrong for a model that must keep state.
must_check: That the gradient axis is logarithmic and states the norm (L2) and whether it is before clipping.
That layers are labelled with the same naming in legend and text.
That features are shown with a symmetric colour scale around zero.
That an embedding figure states the projection method and the separability measure.

terms.meaning: The length of the vector of derivatives of the loss with respect to a group of parameters.
A gradient that shrinks by a factor per layer so early layers barely learn.
Rescale the gradient when its norm exceeds a cap c.
A function of the raw inputs given to the model, such as x squared or sin x.
The vector of activations of a hidden layer for one sample.
A score for how well two classes can be split in an embedding.

remember: The gradient to layer 1 is a product of one factor per later layer; the product shrinks or grows geometrically in depth.
A log axis is needed for gradients because they span many decades.
Clipping changes the step but not the plotted pre-clip gradient.
A model is a combination of its input features; adding x^2 and y^2 lets a linear model draw circles.
Separability of an embedding is not the same as quality of the dynamics.

steps.title: Why depth shrinks the first-layer gradient
steps.tex: \frac{\partial L}{\partial W_1}=\left(\prod_{k=2}^{K}D_k\,W_k\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\frac{\partial L}{\partial y}\,x^{\mathsf T},\qquad D_k=\operatorname{diag}\,\sigma'
steps.note: Each additional layer multiplies the signal by W_k and the activation slopes. If their typical size is below 1 the product falls geometrically with the number of layers; above 1 it blows up.

steps.title: Per-layer factor implied by the figure
steps.note: Read from the plot at epoch 1: eight layers about 0.25, two layers about 20, six extra layers. The result is a rough per-layer shrink factor of about one half. Values are read by eye.

steps.title: Clipping caps the step, not the plot
steps.note: Because the figure plots the norm before clipping, a spike to 20 does not mean a step of that size was taken; it means clipping was active.

steps.title: What a feature filter is
steps.note: Each panel is just the function evaluated on a grid and coloured by sign. A linear model on these seven inputs forms weighted sums of these pictures, so a circle is a sum of the two bowls.

worked.title: Per-layer shrink from two curves
worked.problem: At epoch 1 the first-layer gradient is about 20 for 2 hidden layers and about 0.25 for 8. Estimate the per-layer factor.

solution.text: The ratio over six extra layers.

worked.answer: About 0.5 per layer. With that factor 8 layers keep (0.5)^7 = 0.8 percent of the gradient of one layer.

analyze.q: Why does the sawtooth appear in the gradient curves, and what would you plot to remove it?
analyze.hint: Mini-batch noise; take a running median.

analyze.q: The eight-layer curve jumps by two decades near the end. Name two possible causes and the log you would add to tell them apart.
How could a Neural ODE embedding have lower separability than an MLP and still be better at a rollout?

evaluate.q: Would you accept 'depth is bad' from the two-curve figure?
evaluate.hint: One run; initialization and normalization matter.

evaluate.q: Is the seven-filter picture enough to explain why a model succeeds on the circle dataset?

create: Add a third curve for eight layers with a residual connection and predict its position relative to the other two.
Design a figure that shows per-layer gradient norm as a heat map over layers and epochs, with a symlog or log colour scale.

checks.q: What does a gradient norm of 1e-4 for a layer say?
checks.hint: How far will the weights move?
checks.answer: That layer's parameters receive almost no learning signal; with a normal learning rate they barely move.

checks.q: A layer factor of 0.6 over 10 layers: how much of the gradient remains?
Why are the last-layer weight gradients the largest in the per-parameter figure?
checks.hint: Compare the chain rule for last and first layers.
checks.answer: They are closest to the loss, so they are not multiplied by later layers' shrink factors, and they multiply the full activations.

checks.q: A late rise of all gradients by two decades means the model is learning faster. True?
checks.hint: Look at the loss in the sibling figures.
checks.answer: No: it usually accompanies a loss spike; a larger gradient is a larger step, not better learning.

checks.q: Suggest an intervention to restore gradient flow in the eight-layer network.
checks.answer: Residual connections, normalization layers, a better initialization, or fewer layers; then repeat the figure and compare.
